## Part 1: Programming building blocks

### Loops

A loop is a structure that can run the same code multiple times. 
Here is an example of code that prints "Hello" 10 times. 

```{r}

for(i in c(1:10)){
  print("Hello")
}

```

### Binding dataframes (rbind)
Sometimes you want to combine two dataframes by pasting them below each other.


Here is some code that successfully combines two dataframes x and y

```{r}

x = data.frame(a = c(1:10),
               b = rnorm(10, 0, 1))

y = data.frame(a = c(1:20),
               b = rnorm(20, 0, 1))

z = rbind(x,y)

```

### Joining dataframes (left_join)

Sometimes you want to combine columns of two dataframes based on some specific group

For example, say you have a dataframe with someone's name and age, and another dataframe with name and height.
Here is how you can combine the two dataframes so you have name, age, and height

```{r}

ages = data.frame(
  names = c('Andy', 'Aaroha', 'Eulalie'),
  ages = c(29, 14, 4)
)

heights = data.frame(
  names = c('Andy', 'Aaroha', 'Eulalie'),
  heights = c(5.6, 5, 3)
)

combined = ages %>%
  left_join(heights, by='names')

```

### Reshaping dataframes

Sometimes you want to take a data frame that is in the long format, and make it wide (for example because you want to compute difference between the columns). You can do this with `pivot_wider`

```{r}

x = data.frame(cond = c('A', 'B'),
               val = c(10, 7))


x_wide = x %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = cond,
              values_from= val)


```

## Part 2: Computing bootstrapped CIs

Here is some code that computes boostrapped CI. 

```{r}

n_boots = 100
prefer_boots <- data.frame()

for(i in c(1:n_boots)){
  curr_sample <- house_prices %>%
    group_by(prefer) %>%
    slice_sample(prop=1, replace=TRUE) %>%
    summarise(mean_price = mean(price)) %>%
    mutate(iter=i)
  
  prefer_boots <- rbind(prefer_boots, curr_sample)
}

prefer_boots_summ <- prefer_boots %>%
  group_by(prefer) %>%
  summarise(lower = quantile(mean_price, c(0.025)),
            upper = quantile(mean_price, c(0.975)))


prefer_summ <- house_prices %>%
  group_by(prefer) %>%
  summarise(mean=mean(price)) %>%
  left_join(prefer_boots_summ, by="prefer")


```

## Part 3: Using permutation to compute p-values

Here is some code that computes a p-value to answer the question "Is the mean house price for houses with and without gas heat significantly different?" 

```{r}

## null distribution
n_boots = 1000
null_gasheat <- data.frame()

for(i in c(1:n_boots)){
  curr_null = house_prices %>%
    mutate(gasheat = sample(gasheat, replace=FALSE)) %>%
    group_by(gasheat) %>%
    summarise(mean_price = mean(price)) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from =gasheat, values_from = mean_price) %>%
    mutate(diff = yes-no,
           iter=i)


  null_gasheat = rbind(null_gasheat, curr_null)
}

## true difference
true_gasheat = house_prices %>%
  group_by(gasheat) %>%
  summarise(mean_price = mean(price)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from =gasheat, values_from = mean_price) %>%
    mutate(diff = yes-no,
           iter=i) 


diffs_gasheat = abs(null_gasheat$diff) >= abs(true_gasheat$diff)
pval_gasheat = mean(diffs_gasheat)
print(pval_gasheat)

```
